body.statement:
For every valid finite binary-rational encoding \(\mathfrak E\) and every \(0<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}<1\), the deterministic nested interval Bellman algorithm in the corrected certificate handle terminates and returns rational endpoints, an attained finite-net prior \(\lambda\), and a finite mixture of net Bayes controls \(u\).  Its cumulative lower and upper sequences are respectively nondecreasing and nonincreasing, converge to \(V\), and at termination satisfy
\[
 \underline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon},
 \qquad
 \overline V_{\varepsilon}-\underline V_{\varepsilon}\leq
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}.
\]
The certificate ledger records the actual terminal-regularization, guard-exit, time-discretization, interpolation and control-mesh, Gaussian-cell, Gaussian-tail, oracle and linear-program, recovered-policy, prior-net, and outward-rounding bounds.  The returned mixture is re-evaluated by an independent fixed-policy interval recursion, which certifies \(\max_{1\leq m\leq M}r_m(u)\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}\).  For this returned mixture, boundary-stable transfer gives predictable finite-horizon policies \(\pi_n\) satisfying
\[
 \max_{1\leq m\leq M}r_{n,m}(\pi_n)
 \leq \overline V_{\varepsilon}+o(1)
 \qquad(n\to\infty).
\]
No closed-form mesh size, arithmetic complexity bound, or convergence rate is asserted.
body.justification: The theorem gives a reproducible epsilon certificate because every accepted endpoint is backed by a candidate-specific rational ledger, the primal policy is independently re-evaluated, and termination follows from the proved convergence of the nested lower and upper schemes.
body.gap: The nearest scalar e-value recursion and sparse two-stage enrichment program do not certify this continuum minimax value or its response-adaptive policy mixture; the theorem makes no unsupported closed-form complexity comparison.
body.consumer: The certified interval, least-favorable net prior, and independently checked policy mixture can accompany rpact recruitment tables and interAdapt finite-stage decision rules.
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\ell_{m,\delta}^-\) and \(\ell_{m,\delta}^+\) for the two losses in Definition~\(\mathrm{def{:}terminal\mbox{-}envelopes}\).  The definitions of \(f_\delta^-\) and \(f_\delta^+\) give, for every real \(a\),
\[
 f_\delta^-(a)\leq \mathbf 1\{a<0\}\leq f_\delta^+(a).
 \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for \(a<0\) the middle term and \(f_\delta^+(a)\) equal one and \(f_\delta^-(a)\leq1\); for \(a=0\) the middle term and \(f_\delta^-(a)\) equal zero; and for \(a>0\) the middle term and \(f_\delta^-(a)\) equal zero while \(f_\delta^+(a)\geq0\).  Since the discovery weights are positive and sum to one, (1) yields
\[
 0\leq \ell_{m,\delta}^-\leq \ell_m\leq
 \ell_{m,\delta}^+\leq1.
 \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, if \(c_{m,\delta}^\pm\) denotes the oracle value obtained from \(\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\), then
\[
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)\leq B(\lambda)\leq B_\delta^+(\lambda),
 \qquad
 c_{m,\delta}^-\leq c_m\leq c_{m,\delta}^+.
 \tag{3}
\]
These are inequalities between observed-law control functionals; they do not redefine the causal regret target \(V\) in Definition~\(\mathrm{def{:}minimax\mbox{-}regret}\).

We next establish the regularity used by the interval recursion.  Put \(s_k=x_k-q_k/2\) and \(e_I=|I|^{-1}\sum_{k\in I}\exp(s_k)\).  Along any line segment in \((x,q)\), the composition of either envelope with \(a_j=\min_{I\ni j}e_I-20\) is absolutely continuous.  At almost every point at which its derivative is nonzero, the active intersection satisfies
\[
 19<20-\delta\leq e_I\leq20+\delta<21.
\]
At such a point,
\[
 \sum_{k\in I}\left|\frac{\partial e_I}{\partial x_k}\right|=e_I<21,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k\in I}\left|\frac{\partial e_I}{\partial q_k}\right|=\frac{e_I}{2}<\frac{21}{2}.
\]
The envelope slopes have absolute value at most \(1/\delta\).  Integration along the segment, including the finitely many changes of the minimizing intersection by absolute continuity, therefore proves
\[
 |\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x,q)-\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x',q')|
 \leq \frac{32}{\delta}
 \|(x,q)-(x',q')\|_\infty.
 \tag{4}
\]
No lower bound on a coordinate of \(q\) was used.

For a prior \(\lambda\), the likelihoods in the frozen core give the posterior weights \(b_m^\lambda\).  Along the same segment,
\[
 d\log Z_m=\sum_j h_j^m\,dx_j-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2\,dq_j,
\]
so \(|d\log Z_m|\leq K(H+H^2/2)\|(dx,dq)\|_\infty\).  Differentiating the normalized weights gives
\[
 db_m^\lambda=b_m^\lambda\left(d\log Z_m-
 \sum_r b_r^\lambda d\log Z_r\right),
\]
and hence
\[
 \sum_m|db_m^\lambda|
 \leq2K\left(H+\frac{H^2}{2}\right)
 \|(dx,dq)\|_\infty.
 \tag{5}
\]
This remains valid when some \(\lambda_m\) is zero, because the corresponding posterior weight is identically zero.  Combining (4)--(5), the normalized posterior terminal payoff
\[
 g_{\lambda,\delta}^\pm(x,q)
 =\sum_m b_m^\lambda(x,q)\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm(x,q)
\]
has the uniform modulus
\[
 \Omega_\delta(d)=
 \min\!\left\{1,
 \left(\frac{32}{\delta}+2K\left(H+\frac{H^2}{2}\right)\right)d\right\}.
 \tag{6}
\]
On a guard box, divide the unnormalized reference payoff by a bound \(C_G\geq\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\).  The multiplier \(\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m/C_G\) lies in \([0,1]\) and, by the same log-likelihood calculation, has Lipschitz constant at most \(K(H+H^2/2)\).  Thus the conservative modulus (6) also bounds the scaled reference-law terminal datum used by the interval recursion.

The same modulus controls every finite-stage continuation value.  To see this without a comparison theorem, take two states at the same time and, under each fixed scenario, couple their future noises.  Translate the second policy's observed score-clock history by the difference of the two initial states before feeding it to the first policy.  The two policies then choose the same allocations and their terminal score-clock difference equals their initial difference.  Equation (4) bounds the conditional loss difference, and (5) bounds the difference of the initial posterior mixtures.  Taking an infimum over policies in both directions proves the assertion.  This translation argument is valid on zero-allocation faces because it never divides by an allocation clock.  It also proves the modulus for each exact time-discrete Bellman recursion by backward induction.

We now give the promised direct validation of the regularized Bellman calculation.  Under the zero-drift reference law, bounded predictability makes
\[
 Z_m(X(t),Q(t))=
 \exp\!\left\{\sum_j h_j^mX_j(t)-\frac12\sum_j(h_j^m)^2Q_j(t)\right\}
 \tag{7}
\]
a mean-one likelihood process.  For a simple predictable control this follows by conditioning successively on independent centered Gaussian increments.  For a general progressively measurable control, approximate its square-root coordinates in the stochastic-integral norm by simple predictable processes.  The integrands in (7) are bounded by \(H\), so the exponential second moments are uniformly bounded; the simple-process likelihoods therefore converge in \(L^1\), and (7) remains a mean-one martingale.  Thus, for every bounded terminal variable \(R\),
\[
 \mathbb E_m^u[R]=\mathbb E_0^u[Z_m(X(1),Q(1))R].
 \tag{8}
\]
In particular, the reference-law terminal datum for the Bayes problem is \(\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm\), exactly the datum defining \(F_\lambda\).

Fix temporarily \(\delta\), a finite time partition, and a score guard radius \(G>H\).  On \(\|x\|_\infty\leq G\), (7) is at most \(C_G=\exp(KHG)\).  Divide the reference-law recursion by \(C_G\).  At the first guard exit its conditional continuation is between zero and the current total likelihood divided by \(C_G\), and the latter is at most one because the continuous score hits the guard boundary before leaving it.  Hence \([0,1]\) is a valid exterior interval; no clamped extension of the value is being assumed.

For completeness, we prove the finite-horizon interval induction used by the algorithm.  Suppose every vertex of a viable state cell carries an interval enclosing a continuation value with modulus \(\Omega_\delta\).  If \(y\) lies in that cell and \((\beta_v)_v\) are its multilinear barycentric weights, then \(\beta_v\geq0\), \(\sum_v\beta_v=1\), and
\[
 \left|F(y)-\sum_v\beta_vF(v)\right|
 \leq\sum_v\beta_v\Omega_\delta(\|y-v\|_\infty)
 \leq\Omega_\delta(d),
 \tag{9}
\]
where \(d\) is the cell diameter.  Thus the barycentric interval enlarged by \(\Omega_\delta(d)\) encloses \(F(y)\).

For a time increment \(a>0\), a constant allocation \(v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\), and a standard Gaussian vector \(z\), the reference-law transition is
\[
 (x,q)\longmapsto
 \bigl(x+(av)^{1/2}\mathbin\odot z,\ q+av\bigr).
 \tag{10}
\]
For every retained Gaussian cell, interval arithmetic encloses the whole image of (10).  Multiplication of its nonnegative continuation interval by an outward-rounded probability interval and outward summation therefore preserves enclosure.  The omitted mass is multiplied by \([0,1]\).  If \(v'\) is another allocation, coupling (10) with the same \(z\), the square-root inequality \((\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\leq|p-q|\) gives the computable control-net error
\[
 \mathbb E\,\Omega_\delta\!\left(
 a\|v-v'\|_1+sqrt{a\|v-v'\|_1}\,\|z\|_2
 \right).
 \tag{11}
\]
It tends to zero with the control-net radius, uniformly in \(v\), by bounded convergence.  Taking the minimum of lower endpoints minus (11), and the minimum of upper endpoints plus (11), encloses the Bellman infimum over the whole allocation simplex.  Equations (9)--(11), followed backward through the finite number of time levels, prove enclosure by induction.  They also show that, for a fixed time partition and guard box, the accumulated interpolation, control-net, Gaussian-cell, Gaussian-tail, and rounding widths tend to zero as their respective finite meshes and arithmetic units tend to zero.  The Gaussian cell probabilities are computable with rational outward bounds: on a bounded cell, integrate rational upper and lower Taylor bounds for \(\exp(-z^2/2)\); outside the truncation box, the exponential-moment inequality gives \(\Pr\{|Z|>z\}\leq2\exp(-z^2/2)\).  Both remainders decrease effectively to zero.

It remains to validate passage from the finite time recursion to the continuous control value.  We do this directly rather than assume statewise Hamilton--Jacobi comparison.  Let \(P_a^v\) denote the Gaussian operator in (10), and let
\[
 \mathcal L^v\phi=\frac12\sum_jv_j\partial_{x_jx_j}\phi+
 \sum_jv_j\partial_{q_j}\phi.
 \tag{12}
\]
The operator is linear in \(v\), so its minimum over the allocation simplex is attained at a vertex.

Let \(J_l\) be the exact regularized reference-law value when controls are constant on the intervals of a fixed partition \(0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=1\), with \(a_l=t_{l+1}-t_l\).  Its backward recursion gives, for every \(v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)\),
\[
 J_l\leq P_{a_l}^vJ_{l+1},
 \qquad
 J_l=\min_{v\in\Delta(\mathcal J)}P_{a_l}^vJ_{l+1}.
 \tag{13}
\]
The first inequality, which holds for every action, is the source of the certified lower bound.  In particular, no interchange of convolution and minimization is needed.

Convolve the multilinear lower interpolants on the inner score box with a fixed rational, compactly supported \(C^3\) tensor mollifier of radius \(\kappa\), with support contained in the guard box.  Convolution commutes with every translation-Gaussian operator \(P_a^v\).  If the interval induction has one-layer enclosure error at most \(\xi_l\), subtracting the recursively accumulated quantity \(\sum_{s\geq l}\xi_s\) restores the first inequality in (13) exactly for the smoothed lower interpolants.  Taylor's formula with integral remainder applied to (10) gives, cell by cell,
\[
 P_a^v\phi-\phi-a\mathcal L^v\phi
 =\mathcal R_a^v(\phi).
 \tag{14}
\]
An outward rational bound for \(|\mathcal R_a^v(\phi)|\) is obtained from the interval bounds for the derivatives of the mollified interpolant and the truncated Gaussian moments, with the omitted moment tail entered separately.  For a fixed \(\kappa\), the third-order score remainder is bounded by a computable constant times \(a^{3/2}\kappa^{-3}\), the second-order clock remainder by a computable constant times \(a^2\kappa^{-2}\), and the interpolation contribution by \(\xi_l\).  Hence, after division by \(a\), all these bounds tend to zero whenever
\[
 \max_l a_l\downarrow0,\qquad
 \sum_l\xi_l\downarrow0,\qquad
 \max_l\frac{\xi_l}{a_l}\downarrow0,\qquad
 \kappa\downarrow0,\qquad
 \max_l a_l^{1/2}\kappa^{-3}\downarrow0.
 \tag{15}
\]
Such rational tuples occur in the deterministic nested enumeration; for example, the enumeration contains arbitrarily small time meshes followed by still finer state, control, Gaussian, and arithmetic meshes, and it tests the displayed quantities rather than presuming a rate.  The terminal mollification error is at most \(\Omega_\delta(\kappa)\) by (6).

Linearly interpolate the smoothed lower functions in time, using the exterior lower value zero as the stopped boundary datum.  Equations (13)--(15) then give a computable terminal discrepancy \(e_T\) and a nonnegative piecewise-constant residual \(e_B(t)\) such that
\[
 \phi^-(1,\cdot)\leq C_G^{-1}\sum_m\lambda_mZ_m\ell_{m,\delta}^\pm,
 \qquad \phi^-\leq0\ \hbox{on the guard boundary},
 \qquad
 \partial_t\phi^-+\mathcal L^v\phi^-\geq-e_B(t)
 \quad\hbox{for every }v\in\Delta(\mathcal J).
 \tag{16}
\]
The quantities \(e_T\) and \(\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt\) are outward rational bounds computed from the finite induction.  Under (15),
\[
 e_T+\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{17}
\]
To pass from (16) to expectations, first take a simple control that is constant on finitely many predictable subintervals and stop it at guard exit.  On each subinterval, conditional Gaussian integration and the integral Taylor identity (14) give the expected change of \(\phi^-\); summing these identities telescopes.  Since
\(\mathcal L^u=\sum_j u_j\mathcal L^{e_j}\), the result is that every such simple control has scaled risk at least
\[
 \phi^-(0,0,0)-\int_0^1e_B(t)\,dt.
 \tag{18}
\]
The stopped process and all derivatives used above are bounded on the guard box.  Approximation in (19)--(20), applied before taking the terminal limit, therefore extends the same inequality to every progressively measurable control.  Thus (18) is obtained by finite Gaussian identities and a limit, not by assuming a statewise comparison theorem.

For the upper side, the grid Bellman recursion selects a predictable piecewise-constant control, and the algorithm evaluates that fixed policy anew rather than using its optimizing recursion.  Its interval expectation is therefore an upper bound for its actual risk, and its actual risk is an upper bound for the unrestricted infimum.  These upper bounds approach the unrestricted regularized value.  Indeed, simple predictable simplex-valued processes on deterministic partitions are dense in the following direct sense.  Approximate indicators in the predictable sigma-field by finite unions of left-cylinder rectangles, approximate bounded coordinates by simple functions, and project the resulting vectors onto the simplex.  This produces \(v^{(N)}\) with
\[
 \mathbb E\int_0^1\|u(t)-v^{(N)}(t)\|_1\,dt\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{19}
\]
Using the same Brownian motions and \((\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\leq|p-q|\),
\[
 \mathbb E\|Q^u(1)-Q^{v^{(N)}}(1)\|_1\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \sum_j\mathbb E\left|
 \int_0^1\bigl(\sqrt{u_j(t)}-\sqrt{v_j^{(N)}(t)}\bigr)\,dW_j(t)
 \right|^2\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{20}
\]
The drift difference under every scenario is bounded by \(H\) times the first quantity in (20).  The modulus (4) and boundedness (2) therefore give convergence of every scenario risk, uniformly over the finite scenario set.  Approximating the finitely many values of each simple control by the rational control net and using (11) finishes the policy approximation.  Combining this upper approximation with the certified lower bound (18) and (17) proves, by finite-horizon induction, that the two regularized Bellman endpoints converge to the same continuous-control value.  No limiting partial differential equation, comparison theorem, or uniqueness theorem is used.

At a fixed time partition, the reference-law transition and terminal datum depend on the observed past only through the current score-clock state and its likelihood vector.  Backward conditioning therefore replaces any history-dependent simple control at each stage by a state-dependent action minimizing the same conditional expectation, without increasing Bayes risk.  Thus the finite Bellman recursion searches a sufficient Markov class and the approximation in (19)--(20) applies to its value, not merely to a larger history-dependent class.

There is no hidden forced-exploration premise in this argument.  When \(v_j=0\), (10) leaves both \(x_j\) and \(q_j\) fixed, (11) remains valid, and (12) simply assigns zero coefficient to the corresponding derivatives.

The guard contribution is also explicit.  Under scenario \(m\), write
\[
 X_j(t)=h_j^mQ_j(t)+M_j(t),
 \qquad
 M_j(t)=\int_0^t\sqrt{u_j(s)}\,dW_j(s),
 \qquad 0\leq Q_j(t)\leq1.
\]
For \(b>0\), conditional Gaussian integration verifies that
\(\exp\{\theta M_j(t)-\theta^2Q_j(t)/2\}\) is a nonnegative mean-one martingale for every real \(\theta\).  Apply the frozen cited linear-boundary lemma with \(\theta=b\), \(\beta=\exp(-b^2/2)\), and \(Q_j(t)\leq1\); repeat with \(-M_j\).  This gives
\[
 \Pr_m^u\!\left\{\sup_{t\leq1}|M_j(t)|\geq b\right\}
 \leq2e^{-b^2/2}.
\]
The martingale identity follows first by conditioning for simple predictable controls and then by stochastic-integral approximation for progressively measurable controls.  Because \(|h_j^m|\leq H\), a union bound gives, uniformly over scenarios and controls,
\[
 \Pr_m^u\!\left\{\max_j\sup_{t\leq1}|X_j(t)|>G\right\}
 \leq \beta(G):=2K\exp\!\left\{-\frac{(G-H)^2}{2}\right\},
 \qquad G>H.
 \tag{21}
\]
Replacing continuation values only after guard exit changes any risk in (2) by at most \(\beta(G)\).  Thus all guard uncertainty is charged through (21), and not through a clamping extension.

We now assemble the minimax certificate.  Define
\[
 G(\lambda)=B(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_m
 =\inf_{u\in\mathcal U}\sum_m\lambda_mr_m(u).
 \tag{22}
\]
Since \(0\leq r_m(u)\leq1\),
\[
 |G(\lambda)-G(\lambda')|\leq\|\lambda-\lambda'\|_1.
 \tag{23}
\]
The required rational prior nets are explicit.  For an integer \(D\geq1\), take all vectors \((k_1/D,\ldots,k_M/D)\) with nonnegative integer coordinates summing to \(D\).  This finite set contains every point mass.  Rounding the first \(M-1\) coordinates of any prior downward to multiples of \(1/D\) and assigning the remainder to the last coordinate gives an \(\ell_1\)-error at most \(2(M-1)/D\).  Hence the certified prior-net radius tends to zero as \(D\to\infty\).

The already proved least-favorable-saddle theorem gives
\[
 V=\max_{\lambda\in\Delta_M}G(\lambda).
 \tag{24}
\]
For a prior-net point, (3) gives the rigorous bracket
\[
 B_\delta^-(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{m,\delta}^+
 \leq G(\lambda)\leq
 B_\delta^+(\lambda)-\sum_m\lambda_mc_{m,\delta}^-.
 \tag{25}
\]
By the quantitative terminal-comparison lemma, the width in (25) caused by regularization is at most
\[
 \bigl(B_\delta^+-B_\delta^-\bigr)
 +\sum_m\lambda_m\bigl(c_{m,\delta}^+-c_{m,\delta}^-\bigr)
 \leq2\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\eta).
 \tag{26}
\]
The lemma also gives \(\rho_{H,K}(\delta,\sqrt\delta)\to0\).  If the prior net has \(\ell_1\)-radius \(r_\lambda\), (23)--(25) show that the maximum of the certified lower endpoints is a lower bound for \(V\), while extending the net by \(r_\lambda\) gives a valid dual upper bound.  The point-mass calculations enclose every oracle in (25) by the same validated recursion, so no oracle offset is reused without its own error interval.

For the primal upper bound, enumerate the finitely many grid policies certified to be near-Bayes at a prior-net point and solve the finite rational scenario-risk linear program.  A mixture with weights \(p_s\) has scenario risk \(\sum_sp_sL(u_s,m)\).  The independent fixed-policy recursion gives intervals \([L_m^-,L_m^+]\) for these risks and intervals \([c_m^-,c_m^+]\) for the point-mass oracles.  Therefore
\[
 V\leq\max_m\{L_m^+-c_m^-\}.
 \tag{27}
\]
This proves validity of the recovered-policy upper endpoint independently of the optimization objective that selected the mixture.

Both sides converge to \(V\).  For the lower side this follows from (23)--(26), the regularized Bellman induction, \(r_\lambda\downarrow0\), \(G\uparrow\infty\) in (21), and vanishing Gaussian-tail and rounding bounds.  For the upper side, let \(\lambda^*\) and a finite mixture of its Markov Bayes best responses be the \(a\)-saddle supplied by the least-favorable-saddle theorem.  If \(\bar\lambda\) is a net point with \(\|\bar\lambda-\lambda^*\|_1\leq r_\lambda\), every such best response is \(2r_\lambda\)-Bayes at \(\bar\lambda\), because both its prior-weighted risk and the Bayes value are one-Lipschitz in the prior.  The regularized Bellman induction approximates each of these finitely many Markov controls by grid policies, so all are eventually retained by the near-Bayes enumeration.  Their mixture is feasible for the rational linear program.  Equations (21), (26), and the independent fixed-policy recursion then make the right side of (27) at most \(V+a+o(1)\).  Letting \(a\downarrow0\) proves convergence of the primal upper bounds.

Every candidate computation is finite: it has finitely many time, state, control, prior, and Gaussian cells, all elementary function evaluations are enclosed by terminating rational Taylor calculations, and both linear programs are finite rational programs.  The deterministic enumeration contains candidates with \(\delta\downarrow0\), \(\eta=\sqrt\delta\), guard radius tending to infinity, and all mesh radii, Gaussian omitted mass, and arithmetic units tending to zero in the nested order required after (13).  Hence (18), (20), (23), and the Bellman induction show that the sum of the actual ledger bounds tends to zero.  For the requested positive \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\), some finite candidate therefore has certified gap at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\).  The search reaches it and terminates.  Taking cumulative maxima of valid lower endpoints and cumulative minima of valid recovered-policy upper endpoints makes the two reported sequences monotone without changing validity.  This proves
\[
 \underline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon},
 \qquad
 \overline V_{\varepsilon}-\underline V_{\varepsilon}\leq
 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}},
\]
as well as \(\max_mr_m(u)\leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}\) for the independently evaluated returned mixture.

Finally, the displayed gap implies \(\overline V_{\varepsilon}\leq V+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\), so the returned finite mixture is an \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cert}}\)-optimal diffusion control.  The already proved boundary-stable-frontier theorem transfers the risk vector of each component, and therefore their finite exogenous mixture, to predictable policies \(\pi_n\).  It also gives \(c_{n,m}\to c_m\).  Since \(M\) is finite,
\[
 \max_m r_{n,m}(\pi_n)=\max_mr_m(u)+o(1)
 \leq\overline V_{\varepsilon}+o(1),
\]
which proves the finite-horizon conclusion.
